title: Canopticon
description: Questions researched in depth, and articles written from what the research found.

items.title: Portraiture as a research method: Sara Lawrence-Lightfoot's "painting with words", how it differs from ethnography, and the case against it
items.summary: Portraiture puts the researcher's own judgement at the centre of a study and measures success by whether readers recognise the truth of the portrait, not by whether anyone could repeat it. Its sharpest critic says that leaves no way to check the portraitist; its founder's answer is that a visible self demands more discipline, not less.

items.title: How investigative YouTube video essays are built: the cold open, the late turn to meaning, and the channels that borrow the form without the evidence
items.summary: The strongest forensic video essays open on an artifact, walk through evidence in the order a viewer would experience it, and say what it all means only late in the video. That delayed turn is what persuades, which is why the same structure works just as well for channels whose evidence does not hold up.

items.title: Paying to reach curious readers in 2026: ChatGPT ads, feed ads, paid newsletter recommendations, and the labelling rules
items.summary: ChatGPT now sells self-serve ads, but they cost about 3–8× more per impression than feed ads and are hard to measure, so the cheapest curious readers are still on Meta and Reddit. An ad can be the whole useful answer and still carry its label: the rules draw the line at fake people and hidden sponsors, not at ads that are worth reading.

items.title: How Canada's public-sector employees vote: the Canadian Election Study evidence, Ottawa's ridings, and the union endorsements
items.summary: Public-sector workers in Canada lean modestly left of private-sector workers, and most of that lean belongs to unionized professionals and managers. The city crews whose unions endorse the NDP vote much like their private-sector counterparts, and no released poll gives a party-by-party split to settle it.

items.title: Paying yourself to do your own tasks: what the incentive trials show, and whether an earn-back subscription could work
items.summary: Financial incentives move behaviour while they run, and losses move people more than equal gains. Paying yourself a wage from your own pocket removes most of what the trials rely on; a subscription you earn back by doing the work is a loss-framed stake, and the research rates it the version most likely to work. Nobody has tested it.

items.title: Canadian recessions and the mortgage channel: rate decisions, CMHC, and five decades of housing-led downturns
items.summary: Every major Canadian downturn since 1980 carries a monetary-policy fingerprint, and housing is how the decision reaches people. The clearest case is 1990, where the campaign overshot its own target and Toronto prices did not pass their 1989 peak until 2002.

items.title: Temporary foreign workers and Canadian innovation: what the automation evidence shows, and the study nobody has run
items.summary: The research that says immigration drives innovation studies points-selected skilled migration. Canada's intake since 2016 has been mostly temporary and low-wage, and the causal work on cheap labour runs the other way — a 1% rise in low-skill wages lifts automation patenting 2–5%. The Canadian version of that study has never been done.

items.title: Whey protein in hot black coffee: why it curdles, what the heat-stable versions cost, and what is coming
items.summary: Collagen disappears into a hot cup; whey turns it into pale lumps that smell of sulfur. Coffee's acidity sits almost exactly where whey is least stable, and it is served above the temperature that unfolds the protein. The heat-stable ingredients that exist solve it by cutting the protein up, which makes it bitter.

items.title: Bill C-11 and Canadian creators in 2026: what the CRTC has actually imposed, and what is still a prediction
items.summary: Creators were told the Online Streaming Act would cost them their foreign audiences by teaching recommendation systems that Canadian videos go unwatched. Three years after royal assent the regulator has imposed no discoverability requirement on anyone, the money is stayed by a court, and no study has measured the harm.

items.title: Topping up low wages in Canada: the Canada Workers Benefit, employer capture, and the workers who never file
items.summary: Canada already runs the alternative to a basic income — a refundable credit that tops up low earnings automatically. Two things decide whether it works: employers absorb part of any wage subsidy where no floor exists, and about 9% of eligible earners never file a return.

items.title: How YouTube, Instagram and TikTok rank video in 2026: satisfaction signals, AI content understanding, and penalties for reposting
items.summary: Recommendation feeds have stopped scoring behaviour alone. A language model now watches the content and judges it — better than the crowd-sourced raters it replaced — while reposting is penalised in the ranking itself. Much of what creators are taught describes the system of a decade ago.

items.title: Measuring the economy with new instruments: scraped prices, card-spending trackers and satellite imagery
items.summary: Four old arguments explain why an economy resists being computed, and none of them have gone away. What computation did change is measurement — scraped prices, card records and satellite images that report what is happening weeks before the official numbers do.

items.title: Immigrants, temporary residents and Canada's job growth since 2020: what the Labour Force Survey can and cannot show
items.summary: Nearly all of Canada's post-pandemic job growth went to immigrants and temporary residents. But no Canadian government table publishes that split the way the American one does — every version of the figure is built by hand from an annual series that undercounts the very group it counts.

items.title: Missed workouts and broken streaks: how fast strength, mood and habit actually decay
items.summary: Two weeks away from the gym costs almost nothing in muscle — strength holds and the body keeps a record that makes the regain fast. What drains in that time is mood, dopamine tone and the automatic habit, which is exactly what restarting runs on.

items.title: Alcohol blackouts: how ethanol blocks memory formation, and why drinking speed decides it
items.summary: In an alcohol blackout the drinker is awake, talking and deciding, while the brain's ability to save the night is chemically held shut. Nothing comes back afterwards because nothing was stored — and how fast the drinking goes decides whether it happens at all.

items.title: Fred Hutch's HSV gene therapy in 2026: mouse and guinea-pig results, no human trial, and the antivirals arriving first
items.summary: A gene therapy clears up to 97% of dormant herpes in mice. In the animal that relapses the way people do it clears above 30%, nobody has filed to test it in a person, and the drugs arriving first suppress the virus rather than remove it.

items.summary: A job for anyone who wants one sounds utopian. It has been tried — in an Austrian town, in 83 French territories and across rural India. It works, it costs money, and the design decides whether it is a springboard or a trap.

items.summary: Short-term rentals add flexible supply, and competition lowers prices. Canadian cities banned them anyway — and cut off a tier between a hotel and a lease just as it was forming.

items.title: Heterocrasis

items.title: Pharmakrasis
